_note: Batch 2 — Gospel, all six styles. 36 answers. Nobody else ships this: published mixing material treats gospel as one genre, and almost all of what exists is written for live reinforcement rather than for making a record. Where a claim is corroborated by published sources it is noted in the why; where it is not, the steps say what to listen for so the user can judge it themselves.

questions.q: How do I mix a live choir recorded with four mics?
questions.short: Treat the four mics as one instrument. Bus them, process the bus, and never gate them.
steps: Check polarity on every mic against the pair you trust most before anything else.
Bus all four. Do every EQ and compression move on the bus, not on individual mics.
High-pass the bus at 150–200 Hz, then cut 2–3 dB somewhere between 500 Hz and 1 kHz for the room.
Pan them to match where the sections actually stood, not evenly across the field.
Compress the bus at 4:1 with 4–6 dB so thirty people move as one body.
questions.why: Four mics on one choir capture the same voices at four distances, so every room resonance is picked up four times and sums. Processing on the bus treats that buildup once; processing per mic multiplies both the work and the artefacts. Church-sound sources consistently put the room's own buildup around 500 Hz to 1 kHz, which is higher than the band you would cut on a single voice.
questions.watch: Bleed between the mics is the ensemble sound. Gate it and you are left with four soloists.

genreNotes.gospel-trad: Expect the band in these mics too. Fix the choir and accept the bleed as part of the record.
genreNotes.gospel-african: Percussion bleeds into choir mics heavily. Compress gently or you will pump the congas.

questions.q: How do I stop the Hammond organ swallowing the whole mix?
questions.short: The organ never stops playing, so it has to be ducked automatically rather than balanced once.
steps: High-pass at 180–250 Hz. Far higher than feels right, and it is the single biggest fix.
Sidechain the organ to the lead vocal: 2–3 dB of ducking, 250 ms release.
Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz permanently, where the lead and the choir need presence.
Narrow the organ to 60–70% width so it stops surrounding the listener.
Ride it up in the turnarounds so it still has its moments.
questions.why: A Hammond with drawbars out is sustained harmonics with no gaps by design — that is its job in the arrangement. Nothing else can be given room by moving the organ fader, because the fader position that works under the vocal is silent in the instrumental. Ducking does automatically what the organist does by ear in the room.
questions.watch: Filter too high and you lose the pedal bass holding a traditional arrangement together. Check with the bass muted.

questions.q: How do I control drum bleed in a live church recording?
aliases: everything is in the drum mics
questions.short: Gate the kick and snare only, phase-align everything, and accept the rest as the room.
steps: Check polarity on every drum mic before touching a gate. Half of what sounds like bleed is cancellation.
Gate only the kick and the snare, and only by 10–15 dB. Never gate to silence.
High-pass the toms at 80–100 Hz and gate them harder — they are open and ringing all song.
Leave the overheads and any room mic ungated. They are the record's sense of a real space.
If the organ is loud in the drum mics, fix the organ's level in the room next time, not in the mix.
questions.why: Bleed in a live recording is not noise, it is the room — and a gospel record that sounds like a room is the point. The mics that genuinely need isolation are the two carrying the groove, because their transients compete with the bleed arriving a few milliseconds late.
questions.watch: Aggressive gating on a live kit produces a record that sounds programmed, which is the opposite of what traditional gospel is for.

questions.q: How do I balance one lead singer against a twenty-voice choir?
questions.short: Give the lead a band nothing else is allowed in, and compress the choir until it is a flat bed.
steps: Compress the lead to 5–8 dB so it is consistently present rather than occasionally loud.
Dip the choir 2–3 dB at 3–5 kHz, exactly where the lead's presence lives.
High-pass the choir higher than the lead: 180–200 Hz against the lead's 80.
Give the choir a longer reverb than the lead, which places it behind without lowering it.
Keep the lead drier than everything around it. Dry reads as close.
questions.why: The lead and the choir are the same instrument in the same range, so they mask each other perfectly and no fader position separates them. Removing the overlapping band keeps the choir's size while clearing the lead — turning the choir down would do the opposite, shrinking the arrangement to solve a frequency problem.
questions.watch: Cut the choir's top too hard and the consonants turn to mush. Dip presence, not air.

questions.q: How do I mix a gospel shout section without it turning to mush?
questions.short: Shorten every reverb and tighten every release. At that tempo, decay is the enemy.
steps: Cut all reverb decays to under 1 second, or automate the sends down for the section.
Shorten every compressor release so nothing is still recovering on the next beat.
High-pass the organ and the choir another 50 Hz higher for this section only.
Ride the whole organ down 2 dB and the drums up 2 dB.
Automate rather than re-balancing: the shout is 16 bars, not the song.
questions.why: A shout section runs at double the perceived tempo of the rest of the song, so reverb tails and compressor releases that were musical in the verse now overlap the next two beats. The mush is time-domain, not frequency, which is why EQ never fixes it.
questions.watch: Do not solve this by lowering the choir. The shout is supposed to be overwhelming — it just has to be legible.

questions.q: How do I keep a four-minute vamp interesting in the mix?
questions.short: Automate something every eight bars. The arrangement repeats; the mix must not.
steps: Map the vamp in eight-bar blocks and change one thing in each.
Open the organ's filter or raise its level a decibel per block as the energy builds.
Bring the ad-libs and the choir up progressively rather than setting one level.
Lengthen the reverb slightly across the section so the space grows.
Hold one element back entirely until the last block, then let it in.
questions.why: A vamp holds the listener through repetition and build, not variation. If the mix is static the ear habituates within thirty seconds and the remaining three minutes feel long — the energy in the room came from the performance intensifying, and automation is how that gets onto the record.
questions.watch: Automate too early and you have nowhere left to go. Save the biggest move for the last eight bars.

questions.q: How do I mix a gospel bass that slaps in one bar and walks in the next?
questions.short: Two compressors with different jobs, plus clip gain on the slaps. One compressor cannot serve both.
steps: Clip-gain every slapped bar down 3–4 dB before any processing.
Compressor one, slow: 3:1, 30 ms attack, 3 dB — shapes the walking line.
Compressor two, fast: 6:1, 2 ms attack, 3 dB — catches the slap transients only.
Use a dynamic EQ cutting 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz, triggered only by the slaps.
Keep the low end identical between the two techniques; only the top should change.
questions.why: Slapping and fingerstyle produce completely different transients from the same instrument. A single compressor set for the walking line is overwhelmed by the slaps; set for the slaps it flattens the walk. Splitting the job by speed lets each stage handle what it is good at.
questions.watch: Taming the slap too hard removes the thing the player was doing on purpose.

questions.q: How do I deal with a leaky kick mic in a live church recording?
aliases: kick mic has everything in it
questions.short: Gate it gently and low-pass it hard. You only need the kick's bottom from that mic.
steps: Low-pass the kick mic at 2–4 kHz. Everything above that is bleed you do not need.
Gate by 10–12 dB, keyed off the kick mic itself, with a fast attack and a 100 ms hold.
High-pass at 35 Hz to remove stage rumble the mic picked up through the floor.
Take the click from a layered sample rather than trying to recover it from the bleed.
Check polarity against the overheads before any of this.
questions.why: A kick mic in a live room hears the bass amp, the organ's pedals and the floor. Low-passing it narrows its job to the one thing it does better than any other mic in the room, and a layered click supplies the definition without re-opening the bleed.
questions.watch: Low-passing this far means the kick has no attack of its own. Layer the click before you judge the result.

questions.q: How do I make a traditional gospel mix sound modern without losing the church?
questions.short: Modernise the low end and the top. Leave the mids, the room and the dynamics alone.
steps: Tighten and extend the low end: that is what dates a mix more than anything else.
Add a gentle shelf above 10 kHz for air the older recordings never had.
Clear 200–400 Hz, which is where older gospel records pile up.
Do not over-compress. The dynamic range between verse and shout is the genre.
Leave the room. Removing it makes the record sound programmed, not modern.
questions.why: What reads as dated is almost always a vague low end and a rolled-off top, both of which were limits of the recording chain rather than choices. The mid-range balance and the dynamics were deliberate, and flattening them is what makes a modernised gospel mix sound like a different genre.
questions.watch: Compressing a traditional gospel record to modern loudness removes the build that the arrangement is entirely about.

questions.q: How do I mix tambourine so it cuts without stabbing?
questions.short: High-pass at 500 Hz, cut 6–8 kHz, and compress hard. It needs presence, not level.
steps: High-pass at 400–600 Hz. A tambourine has nothing useful below that.
Cut 3–4 dB at 6–8 kHz, where the jingles become painful.
Compress at 6:1 with 5–8 dB so the loud strikes stop jumping out.
Pan it 20–40% off centre so it stops competing with the snare and the hats.
Add a short reverb to glue it to the kit rather than raising its level.
questions.why: A hand-played tambourine has an enormous dynamic range — a hard strike can be 15 dB above a soft one — so the level that makes the soft hits audible makes the hard ones painful. Compression is doing the real work here; the EQ just removes the band that hurts.
questions.watch: Over-compressed tambourine loses its swing and starts sounding like a loop.

questions.q: How do I mix a Leslie cabinet on a Hammond?
questions.short: Keep the top and bottom rotor mics separate, pan the top pair wide, and leave the drum mono.
steps: Keep the horn (top) mics as a stereo pair and pan them 70–100% out.
Keep the bass rotor (bottom) mic mono and centred.
Do not compress hard. Compression fights the rotor's own amplitude modulation.
High-pass the horn mics at 300 Hz and the drum mic at 60 Hz.
Check phase between the top and bottom mics — they are several feet apart.
questions.why: A Leslie's sound is amplitude and pitch modulation created by two rotors spinning at different speeds. Stereo mics on the horn capture the Doppler sweep that makes it swirl; the bass rotor turns too slowly to produce a useful stereo image and only causes phase trouble when spread.
questions.watch: Compressing a Leslie flattens the rotor's own volume swell, which is the entire effect.

questions.q: How do I keep a live gospel mix exciting when the band gets loud?
questions.short: Automate things down, not up. In the loud sections, subtraction is what creates impact.
steps: Ride the organ, the pads and the reverb returns down 2 dB in the loudest sections.
Push the kick and the lead vocal up 1 dB rather than raising everything.
Shorten reverb decays for the loud passages so the density does not compound.
Keep the verses genuinely quieter — the contrast is what makes the loud parts land.
Check the loudest 16 bars against a reference at matched loudness.
questions.why: When every source is at maximum the ear has no reference for loud, so the section stops feeling big and starts feeling flat. Lowering the sustained elements restores the difference between transient and bed that the ear reads as impact.
questions.watch: The temptation is to raise the vocal to compete. That produces a loud flat mix with a loud flat vocal.

questions.q: How do I blend programmed drums with a live gospel drummer?
questions.short: Put both through one bus, one compressor and one room. Separate processing keeps them separate.
steps: Route the programmed and live kits into a single bus and compress there, 3:1 with 2–4 dB.
Send both to the same room reverb — this is what makes them share a space.
Align the programmed hits to the live drummer's timing, not the grid.
Darken the samples with a low-pass around 12 kHz; programmed drums are usually brighter.
Layer, do not duplicate: if the live snare is good, the sample should only add weight.
questions.why: Two kits sound separate because they are in different rooms and moving on different envelopes. A shared reverb gives them one space, and a shared compressor gives them one envelope — those two cues are what the ear uses to decide whether sounds happened together.
questions.watch: Quantising the programmed parts to the grid when the drummer is not on the grid creates flams on every hit.

questions.q: How do I mix stacked contemporary gospel vocals?
questions.short: One bus, one compressor, one reverb, and pan by voice part rather than by take.
steps: Bus every stack layer and do all processing on the bus.
Compress the bus at 4:1 with 4–6 dB so the whole stack breathes as one.
Pan by part: lowest harmony nearest centre, highest hardest out.
High-pass the bus at 180–220 Hz so eight voices do not crowd the low mids.
Dip 2–3 dB at 3–5 kHz so the lead keeps its presence band.
questions.why: Bus compression gives every layer one shared envelope, so the ear hears a texture rather than counting singers. Panning by pitch keeps the chord readable, because each voice can be followed to its own position — random panning turns the same stack into a wash.
questions.watch: Bus compression pulls up the breaths on every layer simultaneously. Clean them before compressing.

questions.q: How do I get a contemporary gospel mix to compete with secular radio?
questions.short: It is the low end and the vocal level, not the limiter. Gospel mixes are usually both too polite.
steps: Compare against two secular references at matched loudness, not matched fader.
Raise the lead vocal. Gospel mixes habitually sit the vocal 2 dB lower than pop does.
Tighten and extend the low end — this is where most gospel mixes lose the comparison.
Clear 200–400 Hz hard. Live instrumentation fills that band more than programmed production does.
Limit 3–4 dB, not 8. Past that you are trading dynamics for nothing streaming will keep.
questions.why: Streaming normalises to around −14 LUFS, so a loudness contest is unwinnable by design. What actually differs between a gospel mix and a pop mix at the same playback level is low-end control and vocal forwardness, and both are balance decisions made long before the limiter.
questions.watch: Matching a pop reference exactly can strip the live, dynamic feel that makes the record gospel.

questions.q: How do I mix a track that switches from programmed to live halfway through?
questions.short: Share the reverbs and the bus processing across both halves, and cross the transition, not cut it.
steps: Use the same reverb sends for both halves so the space does not change at the switch.
Keep the mix bus chain identical; resist a second set of settings for the live half.
Start the live elements two bars before the programmed ones stop.
Match the vocal's level and tone across the transition before you fix anything else.
Automate one element across the boundary so something is continuous.
questions.why: The ear accepts a change of instrumentation easily and a change of room almost never. Keeping the reverb and the bus constant means the listener hears the band change while the space stays — which is what happens in a real service.
questions.watch: Different halves often need different EQ. Do it on the sources, never on the bus.

questions.q: How do I sit a worship pad under a busy arrangement?
questions.short: Filter both ends hard and duck it under the vocal. A pad should only be missed when it is muted.
steps: High-pass at 250–350 Hz and low-pass at 8–10 kHz.
Sidechain to the lead vocal, 3–4 dB, with a slow release.
Cut 3 dB at 2–4 kHz permanently.
Lower it until you cannot consciously hear it, then mute it to check it is doing something.
If it still clogs the mix, the patch has too many layers — remove one.
questions.why: A pad sustains, so unlike a transient source it never stops contributing low-mid energy. In a busy arrangement that makes it the single largest cause of a mix being muddy for its whole duration, even at a level nobody notices.
questions.watch: Filtering this hard can remove the chord's root. Check it still implies the harmony before moving on.

questions.q: How do I mix gospel keys that double the bass line?
questions.short: Ask the player to stop, or high-pass the keys at 150–200 Hz. There is no third option.
steps: Check whether the left hand is on the same notes as the bass. Usually it is.
High-pass the keys at 150–200 Hz and let the bass own everything below.
If the keys part needs its low end, high-pass the bass at 100 Hz instead and let the keys have it.
Decide which one owns the root. Both cannot.
Cut 2 dB at 250–400 Hz on whichever one lost.
questions.why: Two instruments playing the same note an octave apart do not sum cleanly — small tuning and timing differences create slow beating that reads as mush. This is an arrangement problem, and EQ can only choose a winner rather than solve it.
questions.watch: In traditional gospel the left hand doubling the bass is the sound. Filter rather than remove it.

questions.q: How do I handle a key change in a contemporary gospel mix?
questions.short: Make the bar before it smaller. The lift comes from the drop, not from the rise.
steps: Pull the mix down 1–2 dB in the two bars before the change, or thin the arrangement there.
Open a high shelf on the mix bus by 1 dB from the modulation onward.
Widen the stereo image slightly after the change, not before.
Lengthen the reverb on the vocal from the new key onward.
Add one element that was absent before — that is cheaper than making everything louder.
questions.why: A modulation already raises the pitch, which the ear reads as energy. Raising the level too makes the change loud rather than lifting, and the limiter will take most of it back anyway. Creating space immediately before gives the change somewhere to go.
questions.watch: Automating the mix bus up at a modulation is the most common way to flatten one.

questions.q: How do I make contemporary gospel drums hit like a record?
questions.short: Parallel compression and sample reinforcement. Live gospel kits are recorded too politely.
steps: Layer a sample under the kick and the snare at 20–40% of the live level.
Parallel-compress the drum bus at 10:1, smashed, and blend it under.
Slow every attack time on the bus so transients survive the compression.
Cut 2–3 dB at 300–400 Hz across the kit — live kits in church rooms pile up there.
Clip the loudest transients 2 dB before the limiter ever sees them.
questions.why: Live church kits are recorded in rooms that were built for a congregation, not a record, so they arrive with low transient-to-room ratio. Samples restore the transient and parallel compression restores the density, without removing the live performance underneath.
questions.watch: Too much sample and the kit stops sounding like the drummer who played it.

questions.q: How do I mix a talkbox or vocoder lead in gospel?
questions.short: Treat it as a lead vocal, not a synth: de-ess it, compress it, and keep it centred.
steps: De-ess it. A talkbox produces harsher sibilance than any microphone does.
Compress at 4:1 with 4–6 dB, the way you would a vocal.
High-pass at 150–200 Hz; the carrier synth has low end the part does not need.
Keep it centred and dry if it is carrying the melody; widen it only if it is a pad.
Duck the keys under it — they are usually the carrier's own source.
questions.why: A talkbox is a real vocal tract driving a synth through a tube, so it inherits every vocal problem — sibilance, plosives, inconsistent level — while having none of a microphone's natural rolloff to soften them.
questions.watch: Pitch correction on a talkbox usually sounds worse than leaving it, because the formants are already artificial.

questions.q: How do I stop a contemporary gospel mix crowding in the mids?
questions.short: Count what is in 200–800 Hz. In gospel it is usually seven things, and it should be three.
steps: List every source with energy in 200–800 Hz: keys, organ, guitars, choir, horns, snare, bass.
Pick the three that matter in this song. High-pass the rest at 250–400 Hz.
Give the three remaining sources different centres within the band.
Only then consider a bus cut, and keep it under 1 dB.
Mute each crowded source in turn — the one you miss least should go.
questions.why: Gospel arrangements are mid-dense by nature: organ, piano, choir and horns all live in the same two octaves. No EQ move fixes seven sources competing for one band — the decision about who is allowed in it has to be made before any processing.
questions.watch: High-passing everything at once leaves the mix thin and brittle. Keep three sources with real low mids.

questions.q: How do I make six background vocals feel like a choir?
aliases: make bgvs sound like a choir
questions.short: Width, a long shared reverb and heavy bus compression. Not more layers.
steps: Pan the six parts to six distinct positions rather than three pairs.
Use one hall reverb, 1.8–2.4 s, with 30–40 ms pre-delay, across the whole bus.
Compress the bus at 4:1 with 5–8 dB so individual voices stop being identifiable.
Detune two layers by 4–8 cents to imitate a larger group's pitch spread.
Keep the top end soft — a real choir is darker than six close-miked singers.
questions.why: What makes a choir sound like a choir is that no single voice can be picked out — small pitch and timing differences across many people blur into one body. Compression and detuning imitate that blur; adding more close-miked layers just adds more identifiable singers.
questions.watch: Too much detune and it sounds out of tune rather than large. Stay under 10 cents.

questions.q: How do I mix the modulation into the final chorus?
aliases: how to make the last chorus bigger
questions.short: Add width and length, not level. The limiter will take back anything you add in volume.
steps: Widen the stereo image from the final chorus onward — the extra size reads as bigger.
Lengthen the vocal reverb and raise the sends rather than the faders.
Bring in one element held back until now: a tambourine, a horn line, a new harmony.
Drop the bar before it to almost nothing so the chorus has somewhere to land.
Automate the mix bus high shelf up 1 dB, no more.
questions.why: The master limiter is already holding the loudest sections at the ceiling, so level added to the final chorus is removed again within milliseconds. Width, decay and arrangement density all increase perceived size without touching the peak level the limiter sees.
questions.watch: Widening too far collapses on phone speakers, which is where the last chorus most needs to land.

questions.q: How do I mix a worship song that builds for six minutes?
questions.short: Plan the whole arc before you touch a fader, and start far quieter than feels comfortable.
steps: Map the song in sections and write down a target intensity for each, 1 to 10, before mixing.
Set the first section at the level that leaves room for five more increases.
Increase one dimension per section: elements, width, brightness, reverb length, level.
Hold the biggest move for the final section — not the one before it.
Check the whole arc in one pass without stopping, which is the only way to hear it.
questions.why: A build is a relationship between sections, not a property of any one of them. Mixing section by section always produces a mix that is already at maximum by the third section, because each one sounds better slightly louder than the last.
questions.watch: The most common failure is starting too loud. If section one sounds right in solo, it is probably too big.

questions.q: How do I keep a worship mix intimate in the verse and huge in the chorus?
questions.short: Change the space, not the volume. Dry and narrow reads as intimate; wet and wide reads as huge.
steps: Keep the verse vocal dry, narrow and close — almost no reverb at all.
Open the reverb send and widen the arrangement at the chorus.
Automate the verse reverb's pre-delay long and the chorus's short so the chorus fuses into one wall.
Remove low end from the verse instrumentation and restore it at the chorus.
Keep the vocal's own level roughly constant across both.
questions.why: Intimacy and size are both spatial cues rather than loudness cues. A dry close vocal sounds like someone next to you at any volume, and the same vocal in a long reverb sounds like a room full of people — so you can change the feeling completely without changing the balance.
questions.watch: Raising the vocal at the chorus breaks the illusion. Let the space around it do the work.

questions.q: How do I mix an acoustic-led worship track?
questions.short: The guitar and the voice share one band, so give the guitar the low mids and the voice the presence.
steps: High-pass the guitar at 100 Hz in a band arrangement, or 80 Hz if it is the only instrument.
Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz on the guitar, where the vocal's consonants live.
Let the guitar keep 150–250 Hz; that is its body and the vocal does not need all of it.
Keep both in one shared reverb so they sound like one performance.
Compress the guitar lightly, 3:1 and 2–3 dB. Strum dynamics are the arrangement.
questions.why: With only two sources there is nowhere for either to hide, so the overlap between a strummed acoustic's pick attack and a vocal's consonants becomes the entire mix problem. Dividing the band deliberately is more effective than any amount of balancing.
questions.watch: Over-compressing the guitar removes the dynamic shape that carries a sparse arrangement.

questions.q: How do I mix a congregation mic without it sounding like noise?
questions.short: Band-limit it hard and automate it up only where the congregation is actually singing.
steps: High-pass at 200–300 Hz and low-pass at 6–8 kHz. The useful band is narrow.
Compress at 4:1 with 6–10 dB so it becomes a steady bed rather than a series of events.
Keep it 15–20 dB below the lead. It is texture, not a source.
Automate it up 3–4 dB only in the sections where the room sings, and down elsewhere.
Gate or duck it when the pastor speaks.
questions.why: A congregation mic captures singing, air conditioning, chairs and traffic in roughly equal measure. Band-limiting removes most of what is not voices, and compression turns the remaining irregular events into a continuous presence the ear accepts as a room full of people.
questions.watch: Static congregation level sounds like noise in the quiet sections and disappears in the loud ones.

questions.q: How do I mix two electric guitars both playing ambient swells?
questions.short: Separate them in time and frequency, not just in pan. Two washes in the same band is one wash.
steps: Give each guitar a different delay time — one dotted eighth, one quarter note.
Filter them apart: one high-passed at 300 Hz, the other at 600 Hz with a low-pass on top.
Pan them hard opposite and keep both out of the centre.
Use different reverbs, not one shared send, so they occupy different spaces.
Duck both under the vocal by 2–3 dB.
questions.why: Ambient guitar parts have no transients, so the ear cannot separate them by timing the way it separates rhythmic parts. Different delay subdivisions reintroduce a rhythmic difference, which is what makes two washes audible as two parts.
questions.watch: This is the one place where separate reverbs beat a shared one — shared space fuses them into mud.

questions.q: How do I mix worship vocals so they feel honest, not produced?
questions.short: Keep the breaths, tune gently, and use one compressor instead of a chain of five.
steps: Leave the breaths in. Removing them is the single biggest cause of a vocal sounding manufactured.
Set tuning to 40–60% strength with a slow retune speed, so pitch drift survives.
Use one compressor at 3:1 doing 3 dB, and ride the fader for the rest.
Keep the reverb short and real — a room, not a plate.
Leave the small cracks and catches. They are the performance.
questions.why: Every processor removes some of the variation in a performance, and variation is exactly what the ear reads as a human being rather than a product. Five gentle processors remove more of it in total than one obvious one.
questions.watch: Honest does not mean unprocessed. A fully raw vocal will not sit in a band arrangement.

questions.q: How do I set reverb for a worship ballad?
aliases: how much reverb on a ballad
questions.short: Time the decay to the bar and the pre-delay to a sixteenth. Both come from the tempo, not a preset.
steps: Set the decay so the tail has ended by the next chord change — usually one to two bars.
Set pre-delay to a 1/64 or 1/32 note at the song tempo, typically 25–45 ms at ballad speeds.
High-pass the return at 300 Hz and low-pass at 8 kHz so the tail adds space, not mud.
Use a plate for the lead and a hall for anything behind it.
Duck the return 3–4 dB under the dry vocal so the words always arrive first.
questions.why: A tail that is still sounding when the harmony changes smears two chords together, which is why the right decay is a function of the tempo rather than a taste decision. Pre-delay keeps the dry consonants clear of the tail, so the voice stays intelligible however wet it is.
questions.watch: Long reverb on a ballad is easy to overdo on monitors and impossible to undo at mastering.

questions.q: How do I mix the spontaneous section where nobody knows what happens next?
questions.short: Set a safe static balance, add compression you would not normally use, and ride only the vocal.
steps: Set a balance that works for the quietest and loudest plausible outcome, not the ideal one.
Compress the lead harder than elsewhere, 5–7 dB, so unexpected dynamics stay controlled.
Put a limiter on the mix bus with 3–4 dB of available headroom as a safety net.
Ride only the lead vocal in this section. Leave everything else alone.
Bring the congregation mic up — spontaneity is the one place it genuinely helps.
questions.why: Spontaneous sections defeat detailed automation because there is nothing repeatable to automate against. A conservative static balance with heavier dynamics control fails gracefully in both directions, which is the only useful goal when you cannot predict what arrives.
questions.watch: Over-automating a section like this makes every take sound different and none of them right.

questions.q: How do I stop a worship mix peaking too early?
aliases: everything is loud by verse two
questions.short: Mix the loudest section first, then work backwards making everything before it smaller.
steps: Find the biggest section and mix that one first, with the limiter already in place.
Then mix every earlier section to be measurably smaller than it.
Remove elements from the early sections rather than lowering them.
Check the arc by listening to only the first bar of each section back to back.
Resist fixing a quiet verse by raising it — that is the mistake you are trying to avoid.
questions.why: Mixing in song order means each section is judged against the one before, and each one sounds better slightly louder — so the arc inflates until there is nothing left for the ending. Starting at the ceiling makes everything else a subtraction, which cannot inflate.
questions.watch: Verses mixed this way can feel too small in solo. Judge them in sequence, never alone.

questions.q: How do I mix a worship leader who sings quietly then belts?
aliases: singer goes from quiet to loud
questions.short: Automate the level, then compress. Compression alone cannot cover a 20 dB performance.
steps: Clip-gain every phrase so the quiet and loud sections peak within 4–5 dB of each other.
Then compress at 4:1 with 3–5 dB for the detail within phrases.
Use dynamic EQ at 2–4 kHz triggered only by the belted notes — those get harsh, the quiet ones do not.
Automate the reverb send down on the belts and up on the quiet lines.
Keep a little dynamic contrast. Flattening it entirely removes the performance.
questions.why: A singer going from breath to full voice changes timbre, not just level — the loud notes have far more 2–4 kHz energy. A compressor levels the amplitude and leaves the tonal difference, which is why heavily compressed dynamic vocals sound harsh on the loud lines.
questions.watch: Compressing hard enough to level this by itself will make the quiet lines sound like they were shouted.

questions.q: How do I balance piano and pad when they sit in the same range?
questions.short: Give the piano the transients and the pad the sustain. Filter them into different octaves.
steps: High-pass the pad at 300 Hz and let the piano keep 150–300 Hz.
Low-pass the pad at 8 kHz and let the piano keep the air above it.
Narrow the piano to 60% and leave the pad wide, so they occupy different space.
Duck the pad 2 dB under the piano's attacks with a fast sidechain.
If they still fight, one of them is unnecessary.
questions.why: A piano and a pad voiced in the same register are nearly identical in spectrum, so panning alone cannot separate them. What genuinely differs is their envelope — the piano has attack and decay, the pad has neither — so giving the piano the transient bands and the pad the middle lets each do what only it can.
questions.watch: Filtering the pad this hard can leave it sounding like a telephone. Check it alone before committing.

questions.q: How do I mix a worship track for in-ear monitors and for release?
questions.short: They are different jobs. Build the release mix from the multitrack, never from the monitor mix.
steps: Start the release mix from scratch. An in-ear mix is optimised for playing, not listening.
In-ears need the click and the player's own instrument loud; the record needs neither.
Expect the monitor mix to be drier — players need clarity, records need space.
Keep the same source edits and tuning across both so the performance matches.
Never send a monitor mix to mastering, however good it sounded in the room.
questions.why: A monitor mix exists so musicians can play together, which means it prioritises timing cues over balance and gives each player a different perspective. A release mix has one listener who is not playing anything — almost every decision that helps the first harms the second.
questions.watch: Reusing the monitor mix because it sounded good on stage is the fastest way to a record with no depth.

questions.q: How do I mix African percussion against a programmed kit?
questions.short: Share one room reverb and one bus compressor, and let the live parts keep their dynamics.
steps: Bus the percussion and the programmed kit together and compress lightly, 3:1 and 2–3 dB.
Send both to one short room reverb — this is what puts them in the same place.
Compress the percussion less than you would the kit; the hand dynamics are the groove.
High-pass every percussion part at 200–300 Hz so they stay out of the kick's way.
Darken the programmed samples slightly; they are usually brighter than real skins.
questions.why: Programmed drums arrive with no room at all and hand percussion arrives with plenty, so they read as two separate recordings however well they are balanced. A shared reverb and a shared compressor supply the two cues — one space, one envelope — the ear uses to fuse them.
questions.watch: Compressing hand percussion as hard as programmed drums kills the velocity variation that makes it human.

questions.q: How do I mix a talking drum?
questions.short: Do not gate it and do not compress it hard. The pitch bend is the instrument.
steps: High-pass at 120–180 Hz, lower than other percussion — it has real low end.
Compress gently, 3:1 with 2–3 dB, and use a slow attack so the strike survives.
Never gate it. The decay carries the pitch bend that makes it speak.
Pan it 20–40% off centre, opposite the shaker.
Lift 2 dB at 1.5–3 kHz for the slap, which is where it cuts through a full band.
questions.why: A talking drum's whole identity is the player squeezing the tension cords to bend pitch across the note's decay. Gating or fast compression truncates exactly the part of the sound that carries the bend, leaving something that hits but does not speak.
questions.watch: Treating it like a tom — gate, hard compress, heavy EQ — removes everything that distinguishes it from a tom.

questions.q: How do I balance a choir against African percussion?
questions.short: They collide at 2–5 kHz. Dip the percussion there and let it keep everything above 8 kHz.
steps: Cut 2–3 dB at 2–5 kHz on the percussion bus, where choir consonants live.
Let the percussion keep its top above 8 kHz — that is where shakers and bells do their work.
High-pass the choir at 180–200 Hz so it stops competing with the congas.
Compress the choir harder than the percussion so it stays continuously present.
Pan the percussion wide and keep the choir's centre clear.
questions.why: Hand percussion and choir consonants both peak between 2 and 5 kHz, so the two mask each other in exactly the band that carries intelligibility. The bands above and below are uncontested, which is why trading the presence region costs neither part anything it needs.
questions.watch: Dipping the percussion too far makes it sound like it is behind a curtain while still being loud.

questions.q: How do I stop a shekere masking the hi-hats?
questions.short: Pick one to own 8–12 kHz. Split them by band and by pan, then mute whichever loses.
steps: Decide which one carries the groove. In African gospel it is usually the shekere.
Give the winner 8–12 kHz and low-pass the other at 9 kHz.
Pan them opposite, at least 40% apart.
Compress the shekere at 4:1 so its loud strikes stop punching through the hats.
If both still fight, the arrangement has two parts doing one job.
questions.why: A shekere and a hi-hat are both broadband noise sources peaking in the same octave, so unlike pitched instruments they cannot be separated by frequency content alone — there is no fundamental to move. Only position and bandwidth are available.
questions.watch: Low-passing hats below about 8 kHz makes them sound like they are in another room.

questions.q: How do I make the guitar and percussion lock in a gospel highlife groove?
questions.short: Match their transients and their reverb. Locking is a timing and space problem, not a level one.
steps: Line up the guitar's pick attacks against the percussion's strongest hits; nudge, do not quantise.
Give both the same short room reverb so they occupy one space.
Match their compression attack times so both transients arrive with the same shape.
Pan them close enough to be heard as one gesture, 30–40% apart, not hard opposite.
Cut 2 dB at 2–3 kHz on whichever is less important so their attacks stop competing.
questions.why: In highlife and African gospel the guitar is a percussion instrument that happens to have pitch, and the groove is the interlock between its pattern and the hand drums. The ear judges that interlock from transient timing and shared space, both of which processing can destroy without changing a single level.
questions.watch: Quantising either part to the grid breaks the push-and-pull the style depends on.
